legacyBehavior: Deletion and the dashboard read ad.status, a field that does not exist on the row, so running ads were always deletable and every dashboard bucket collapsed into one undefined key.
replacementBehavior: Every read and write goes through the canonical Status column at a single Prisma boundary.
reason: The guard and the dashboard breakdown must act on the value actually stored.

legacyBehavior: Analytics counters and budget were read outside any transaction and written back whole, losing concurrent increments; budget exhaustion assigned the lowercase status field, which Prisma rejects, so an exhausted ad errored instead of completing.
replacementBehavior: Counter updates re-read inside a Serializable transaction with up to three P2034 retries, and completion is written through Status.
reason: Impression, click, and conversion counts drive billing and must not be lost or error on exhaustion.

legacyBehavior: The raw request body was forwarded to prisma.ad.update, so a caller could overwrite advertiserId, analytics, and review state.
replacementBehavior: Updates are parsed against a strict allowlist that names any rejected field.
reason: Ownership, analytics, and review state must not be caller-writable.

legacyBehavior: AdminJS accepts a known fallback cookie secret.
replacementBehavior: Startup rejects missing production admin session secrets.
reason: A public fallback secret permits session forgery.

legacyBehavior: Blocking and privacy response middleware run before mounted route handlers.
replacementBehavior: Nest guards and serializers enforce blocking/privacy at effective handler boundaries.
reason: The legacy ordering can be ineffective or bypass expected response filtering.

legacyBehavior: The listing included a creator relation that does not exist on the Challenge model, so Prisma raised a validation error and the route returned 500 on every call.
replacementBehavior: The listing includes the real user relation and is projected as creator, so the documented response shape is preserved and the route works.
reason: An always-failing route cannot be migrated as-is.

legacyBehavior: Duets, votes and highlights were read-modify-writes on a JSON column outside any transaction, so concurrent requests silently dropped one another's entries.
replacementBehavior: Each append runs in a Serializable transaction with a bounded retry on P2034, and surfaces a CONFLICT the client can retry rather than losing the write.
reason: Silent data loss under ordinary concurrency.

legacyBehavior: The voter identity was read from req.body.userId, so any authenticated caller could cast a vote as any other user, and could bypass the one-vote-per-user dedupe by sending different ids.
replacementBehavior: The voter is always the authenticated session principal. userId in the body is accepted and ignored so existing clients keep working, and the dedupe is now a real one-vote-per-user rule.
reason: Impersonation and unbounded ballot stuffing on a user-visible counter.

legacyBehavior: Idempotency was a findFirst on the stored reference followed by a create, with no transaction between them, so two verifications of the same reference arriving together both passed the check and both credited.
replacementBehavior: The duplicate check, the balance change and the ledger row happen in one Serializable transaction with a bounded P2034 retry, so a reference credits exactly once.
reason: A repeated provider callback could credit a purchase twice.

legacyBehavior: The new balance was computed in application code from a value read before the transaction and written back as an absolute total, so two credits landing together silently overwrote one another.
replacementBehavior: The balance is incremented inside the transaction, so concurrent credits both land.
reason: Silent loss of purchased coins under ordinary concurrency.

legacyBehavior: A credit was granted on the provider status alone; the amount and currency that actually settled were never compared with the package price.
replacementBehavior: A credit is refused unless the settled amount and currency match the catalogue price for the package named in the provider metadata.
reason: Coins could be credited for a payment that did not cover them.

legacyBehavior: A replayed verification reported the balance read live from the user row.
replacementBehavior: The replay reads the live balance inside the settlement transaction rather than echoing the ledger row balanceAfter, which is history and goes stale as soon as the buyer spends.
reason: Keeps the replay response truthful, matching legacy.

legacyBehavior: Comment likes read the likes JSON array and wrote it back whole with no transaction, losing concurrent likes.
replacementBehavior: The like runs in a Serializable transaction with bounded P2034 retry and dual-writes the CommentLike row, per Plan C step 3. Liking stays idempotent: there is no unlike route in the legacy API.
reason: Like counts must not be lost, and the relational table must stay in step during the dual-write window.

legacyBehavior: Comment routes applied a blocking middleware but never checked that the parent post was visible, so a private post's thread could be read and written by anyone holding the post id.
replacementBehavior: Every comment read and write resolves the shared post visibility policy first and reports NOT_FOUND when denied.
reason: A private post's discussion is as sensitive as the post.

legacyBehavior: Both comment reads fetched every comment and every nested reply with no limit, and creating a comment selected the entire comments relation only to size a counter.
replacementBehavior: Both reads are bounded by a page query and the counter uses a count query; the response stays a bare array.
reason: An unbounded thread read is an availability risk on a popular post.

legacyBehavior: Deleting a community removed every membership row but left memberCount at its previous value, so a reactivated community reported members that no longer existed.
replacementBehavior: The count is zeroed with the deletion, and the cutover backfill resets counts that have already drifted.
reason: A stored counter contradicted the rows it counts.

legacyBehavior: The golden tick was read off a possibly-missing user row, so a deleted user answered 500.
replacementBehavior: A missing user is reported as not found.
reason: An unguarded read on a nullable row.

legacyBehavior: The membership was created and the member count incremented without any gate on whether the row was new, so a racing double join produced two increments.
replacementBehavior: The unique constraint on communityId and userId decides, inside a Serializable transaction, so one row and one increment result.
reason: A user-visible counter drifted under ordinary retries.

legacyBehavior: The search term defaulted to an empty string, so the listing ran three predicates including two case-insensitive contains scans against every row even when no term was given. Page size was also unbounded.
replacementBehavior: An absent term drops the filter entirely, and page size is capped at 100.
reason: Needless full-table scans and an unbounded page size.

legacyBehavior: A paid membership was written only into the communities.members JSON, while every request path reads the relational community_members table. A member who paid was absent from the community detail, refused by the post guard, told they were not a member on leave, and could be sold the same membership again by join.
replacementBehavior: Settlement dual-writes both halves, with the relational row authoritative and deciding whether the member count moves. The JSON keeps being written so anything outside this migration still reading it keeps working. A backfill in the legacy cutover repairs memberships paid for before the cutover.
reason: The paid feature failed to grant what was paid for on every route except the one that recorded the payment.

legacyBehavior: Every community id was validated with isMongoId(), but community ids are uuids. A thirty-six character uuid can never satisfy a twenty-four hex character check, so all three community payment routes answered 400 for every real community.
replacementBehavior: The id is validated as the bounded string it actually is.
reason: Three always-failing routes cannot be migrated as-is.

legacyBehavior: Both post routes included user and community on Post, neither of which is a relation name there, so Prisma rejected the query and both answered 500 on every call.
replacementBehavior: The includes use users_posts_userIdTouser and communities, the same relation names the migrated posts domain already uses.
reason: Two always-failing routes cannot be migrated as-is.

legacyBehavior: Both handlers resolved the caller membership through include: { memberships }, a relation that exists on Community in neither schema, so Prisma rejected the query and both routes answered 500 on every call.
replacementBehavior: Membership is read through the real community_members relation.
reason: Two always-failing routes cannot be migrated as-is.

legacyBehavior: Community-profile documentation and runtime ownership checks do not consistently agree.
replacementBehavior: Typed policies enforce the approved owner/moderator contract.
reason: Authorization behavior must match the public contract.

legacyBehavior: The settings merge read the current settings outside the update that overwrote them, so two concurrent updates lost one of the changes.
replacementBehavior: The read and the write happen in one Serializable transaction.
reason: Silent loss of a configuration change.

legacyBehavior: handleCommunityPaymentSuccess read the completed status outside the transaction that writes it, and credited community earnings by adding to a JSON total read earlier, so a redelivered webhook added a second membership, inflated the member count and credited the earnings twice, while two settlements landing together could lose one of the credits.
replacementBehavior: Settlement is one Serializable transaction whose gate is a conditional update from pending to completed; the membership grant, the User.communities sync and the earnings credit all happen inside it, and the earnings are read in the same transaction that writes them.
reason: A redelivered provider callback granted a duplicate membership and double-credited community earnings.

legacyBehavior: Stripe initialisation never persisted the PaymentIntent id, and verification then asked Stripe to resolve the COMM- prefixed reference, which is not a Stripe id, so Stripe community verification failed on every call.
replacementBehavior: The PaymentIntent id is recorded on the transaction at initialisation and verification asks Stripe about that reference.
reason: An always-failing payment path cannot be migrated as-is.

legacyBehavior: The available balance was read and validated outside the write that reserves against it, so two withdrawals racing each other could both pass a check against the same balance and overdraw it.
replacementBehavior: The balance is read and the reservation written inside one Serializable transaction.
reason: A community could be made to pay out more than it had earned.

legacyBehavior: Database connection failure is logged and swallowed during startup.
replacementBehavior: Readiness fails and bootstrap rejects when Prisma cannot connect.
reason: A listening process must not claim readiness without its database.

legacyBehavior: scores and votes were read, mutated in memory, and written back whole with no transaction, so concurrent updates silently overwrote one another.
replacementBehavior: Both counters are re-read and written inside one Serializable transaction with bounded P2034 retry.
reason: Concurrent scoring and voting must not lose writes.

legacyBehavior: The public listing issued one user query per debate row to resolve participants, and limit was unbounded.
replacementBehavior: Participants for the whole page are resolved in one query and limit is capped. The route stays public, as it was.
reason: A public unbounded read with per-row queries does not survive growth.

legacyBehavior: Any authenticated user could drive the AI scorer against any debate and overwrite a participant score; the handler performed no authorization at all.
replacementBehavior: Scoring requires the debate creator or an administrator, and the score write runs in a Serializable transaction.
reason: A debate outcome must not be settable by an unrelated user.

legacyBehavior: votes is a counts map keyed by participant with no record of who voted, so one user can vote without limit by repeating the request.
replacementBehavior: NOT YET CORRECTED. Closing this needs somewhere to record the voter, which means a DebateVote(voterId, debateId, participantId) table with a unique constraint — a schema migration outside this domain plan. Changing the stored shape instead would break every client reading votes[participantId] as a number. The lost-update half of the defect is fixed; the ballot-stuffing half is carried here.
reason: Recorded as an open gate rather than counted as corrected.

legacyBehavior: Jobs and chain configuration load before dotenv initialization.
replacementBehavior: Validated configuration loads before providers and scheduled jobs.
reason: Import-time provider configuration must not observe missing environment values.

legacyBehavior: Wallet history calls an explorer method that does not provide the documented history contract.
replacementBehavior: The supported explorer history API is used through a typed adapter.
reason: The incompatible method call fails or returns the wrong shape.

legacyBehavior: The route compared the response envelope status to successful, but the envelope reads success for every answered call and the transaction state lives under data.status, so the route could never report a settled payment.
replacementBehavior: The transaction state is read from data.status.
reason: An always-failing route cannot be migrated as-is.

legacyBehavior: Swagger documents a health route that the Express router does not mount.
replacementBehavior: Nest exposes explicit liveness and readiness endpoints.
reason: Operational documentation must describe executable routes.

legacyBehavior: Photo and video editing were mounted without authentication, accepted unbounded uploads validated only by declared MIME type, derived output names from the uploaded filename, wrote them synchronously, and returned raw Sharp and FFmpeg errors including absolute paths.
replacementBehavior: Both routes require a session, bound uploads at 10 MiB and 100 MiB, verify magic bytes against the declared type, generate random output names under one configured root, invoke FFmpeg with shell:false and a fixed argument array under a 60-second timeout, and return a fixed unavailable message.
reason: Anonymous callers must not be able to spend CPU, memory, and disk or learn server paths.

legacyBehavior: Express owns duplicated Passport Google callbacks, bcrypt/JWT credential flows, verification codes, reset tokens, token cookies, and handwritten two-factor/session middleware.
replacementBehavior: Better Auth exclusively owns /api/auth/** with native email/password, conditional Google, bearer, two-factor, verification, reset, cookie, and session contracts; Nest authorization consumes only immutable typed principals.
reason: One native protocol owner removes duplicated credential logic, prevents partial two-factor principals, preserves CSRF/origin defenses, and revokes sessions after password reset.

legacyBehavior: Some legacy handlers reference Prisma delegates absent from the schema.
replacementBehavior: Handlers use only generated delegates or explicit compatible repositories.
reason: A nonexistent model delegate causes deterministic runtime failure.

legacyBehavior: The page size was parsed with no ceiling, so one request could ask for an entire table.
replacementBehavior: Page size is capped at 100; the legacy defaults of 20 and 10 are unchanged.
reason: An unbounded page size is a denial-of-service lever.

legacyBehavior: The computed HMAC was compared with the header using a plain inequality, which is not constant-time, and the header was used without checking it is a string.
replacementBehavior: Comparison is timingSafeEqual over equal-length buffers of the raw request bytes, with a non-string or wrong-length header rejected outright.
reason: A non-constant-time comparison on a signature is a timing oracle.

legacyBehavior: Post anchoring and mint preparation do not consistently enforce post/signing ownership.
replacementBehavior: Authenticated post ownership and signing-address binding are required.
reason: Chain preparation must not authorize another userâ€™s content or address.

legacyBehavior: Like and bookmark read the likes JSON array and engagement outside any transaction and wrote them back whole, losing concurrent updates. Share-to-status carried an explicit allow-sharing comment and performed no access check, copying a private post into a status. Repost applied no visibility check. Promote coerced budget with Number(), admitting NaN and negative values.
replacementBehavior: Every write interaction resolves visibility first and runs in a Serializable transaction with bounded P2034 retry; promotion input is validated.
reason: Interaction counts drive ranking and billing, and a private post must not be republishable by a stranger.

legacyBehavior: Four handlers include a Post relation named user, which does not exist on the model; the author relation is users_posts_userIdTouser. Every reachable call raises a Prisma validation error and returns 500.
replacementBehavior: One Prisma boundary selects the real author relation and projects it as user for clients.
reason: A permanently failing endpoint is not parity.

legacyBehavior: GET /api/posts/:postId checked blocking but never post privacy, so any authenticated caller who knew an id could read an only_me, followers, or select_users post. GET /api/posts/:postId/reposts applied neither privacy nor blocking.
replacementBehavior: Both reads apply the shared visibility policy, and a denied read is reported as NOT_FOUND so an id cannot be probed.
reason: A private post must not be readable by identifier.

legacyBehavior: Some webhook and community-profile paths use incompatible Prisma imports.
replacementBehavior: All migrated handlers inject the single typed Prisma service.
reason: Incorrect import shapes fail deterministically at runtime.

legacyBehavior: Some handlers return raw internal exception messages.
replacementBehavior: The global exception filter returns stable safe errors with correlation IDs.
reason: Internal errors can expose implementation and provider details.

legacyBehavior: Helmet is imported but not installed as active middleware.
replacementBehavior: Compatible Helmet security headers are installed globally.
reason: The runtime should apply the security headers its dependency implies.

legacyBehavior: Legacy short-circuited only on a completed status, so a transaction marked failed during initialisation was still settled if the payer went on to pay.
replacementBehavior: The atomic claim gates on not-completed rather than on pending, preserving that behaviour. Gating on pending would have taken the money and granted nothing whenever initialisation marked the row failed but the payer completed a checkout that was already open.
reason: Guards the migration against narrowing an idempotency gate into a money-losing one.

legacyBehavior: Duplicate method/path declarations in post routing shadow later handlers.
replacementBehavior: One reviewed Nest owner implements each effective post method/path contract.
reason: Declaration shadowing makes later code unreachable or ambiguous.

legacyBehavior: Adding a highlight required only a session; there was no check that the caller hosted the space, so any user could append highlights to anyone else's space.
replacementBehavior: Highlights are host-only, matching the end route. Administrators are not exempt, because a space is host-owned content.
reason: Unauthorized write to another user's content.

legacyBehavior: Reacting read the reactions JSON array and wrote it back whole with no transaction, losing concurrent reactions.
replacementBehavior: The append runs in a Serializable transaction with bounded P2034 retry. Append semantics are unchanged: repeat reactions from the same user are still recorded, and an expired status still accepts a reaction, both as in Express.
reason: Concurrent reactions must not overwrite one another.

legacyBehavior: GET /api/status loaded every unexpired status in the system with no limit, then evaluated blocking one row at a time with a query per status.
replacementBehavior: The query is bounded by a page limit and the blocked set is resolved once per request.
reason: A global unbounded read with per-row blocking queries does not survive growth.

legacyBehavior: Initialization never persisted the PaymentIntent id, and verification then called paymentIntents.retrieve with the SUB- prefixed reference, which Stripe cannot resolve, so Stripe subscription verification failed on every call.
replacementBehavior: The PaymentIntent id is recorded on the transaction at initialization and verification asks Stripe about that reference.
reason: An always-failing payment path cannot be migrated as-is.

legacyBehavior: The transaction id was read off event metadata without a null check, so an event carrying no metadata threw and answered 500, making Stripe retry a request that could never succeed.
replacementBehavior: An event with no transaction metadata is acknowledged as nothing to do.
reason: A permanent 500 on a webhook wastes the provider retry budget.

legacyBehavior: handleSubscriptionPaymentSuccess read the completed status outside the transaction that writes it, so a webhook and a verification racing each other both proceeded and the subscription was extended twice.
replacementBehavior: Completion is one Serializable transaction whose gate is a conditional update from pending to completed; the caller that loses the race is told the work was already done.
reason: A duplicated provider callback extended a paid subscription twice.

legacyBehavior: Subscription expiry invokes an email path with a known incompatible service contract.
replacementBehavior: The scheduled job calls the typed email provider with its supported contract.
reason: The current invocation can fail instead of notifying expiring subscribers.

legacyBehavior: The request body was passed straight into the ORM update, so an administrator could rewrite id or createdAt or drive relation operations, and an unknown key answered 500.
replacementBehavior: Only the columns the route documents are accepted, each optional so a partial update stays partial.
reason: Unvalidated passthrough into an ORM update.

legacyBehavior: The route selected prideTick and businessTick, neither of which is a column on User in either schema, so Prisma rejected the query and the route answered 500 on every call.
replacementBehavior: Both are dropped from the projection; goldenTick, which is a real column, is kept.
reason: An always-failing route cannot be migrated as-is.

legacyBehavior: A user can bind a supplied wallet address without proving control of it.
replacementBehavior: Wallet binding requires nonce-based ownership proof tied to the authenticated user.
reason: Unproven address binding creates asset and identity risk.

legacyBehavior: Webhook verification lacks complete idempotency and replay protection.
replacementBehavior: Raw-body signatures, event identity, idempotency, and replay windows are enforced.
reason: Payment side effects must be authentic and exactly-once at the application boundary.
